topics.name: Similes and comparisons (like, as ... as, -er than)
Prepositions of movement (into, through, across, along)

options: The clouds were as soft than cotton.
The clouds were soft as like cotton.
The clouds were as soft as cotton.
questions.rule: A simile with as uses the pattern as + adjective + as: as soft as cotton.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct verb.
options: Then the drop fall down as rain.
Then the drop fell down as rain.
Then the drop falled down as rain.
questions.rule: Fall is irregular. Its past form is fell, not falled.

options: The tap dripped noisy all night.
The tap dripped noisily all night.
The tap dripping noisily all night.
questions.rule: An adverb (noisily) tells how an action happens. The past tense here is dripped.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: To go from one side of a forest to the other inside it, use through.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Yesterday shows the past, so use the simple past: rained.
The pattern is as ... as: as shiny as a bead.
To describe the verb pushed, use the adverb suddenly.
Subject + past verb + place: The rain fell on the ground.
Short past answer: I closed it. After did, the verb would be the base form close.
The past of bat is batted, and how he batted needs the adverb carefully.

options: The boat sailed across the lake.
The boat sailed across of the lake.
The boat sailing across the lake.
questions.rule: Across means from one side to the other and needs no of: sailed across the lake.

options: Her hands were as cold like ice.
Her hands were cold as like ice.
Her hands were as cold as ice.
questions.rule: Use either as cold as or cold like, never mix as and like.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: To tell how it moved, use the adverb gently.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Last monsoon is past. Rise is irregular: rise - rose - risen.
Along shows movement following a line, like a stream or road.
The sentence needs a full verb in the past: the wind pushed.

questions.prompt: Make a simile about the clouds.
questions.rule: A simile compares two things using like or as: soft like cotton.
An adverb of manner like patiently usually goes after the verb (or just before it): waited patiently for the rain.

options: It rolled under of the sofa.
questions.rule: Under needs no of, and the past tense is rolled.

chat: How was the water in the river?
options: It was as cold than ice!
It was as cold as ice!
questions.rule: Equal comparison: as cold as. Than goes only with -er forms (colder than).

options: The drop splash loudly into the basin.
The drops splashes loudly into the basin.
The drop splashed loudly into the basin.
questions.rule: Past tense splashed + adverb loudly. One drop splashed; drops splashes breaks agreement.

options: The river is wider than the stream.
The river is more wide than the stream.
The river is wider as the stream.
questions.rule: Short adjectives add -er: wider, and -er is followed by than.

options: The children feeled happy when it rained.
The children felt happy when it rained.
The children felt happy when it rain.
questions.rule: Both actions are past: felt (irregular past of feel) and rained.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Moving from outside to inside something uses into: dived into the river.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Spoke how? Use the adverb politely: so politely that everyone liked her.

questions.after: over our water tank every morning.
questions.rule: Fly is irregular: fly - flew - flown. Flown needs has/had.
Often is an adverb of frequency and comes before the main verb. Oftenly is not a word.
Out of shows movement from inside to outside.

chat: Where did the rainwater go after it fell?
questions.rule: Go is irregular; its past form is went.
How she sings needs the adverb beautifully; she takes sings.

options: Yesterday, a small drop fell into a empty bucket.
Yesterday, a small drop falls into an empty bucket.
Yesterday, a small drop fell into an empty bucket.
questions.rule: Yesterday needs the past fell, and empty starts with a vowel sound, so an.

options: The leaves shines like silver after the rain.
The leaves shine like silver after the rain.
The leaves shine as silver like after the rain.
questions.rule: Plural leaves takes shine, and the simile uses just like.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: To tell how they were playing, use the adverb happily.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Use on with days: on Monday morning.
Last night is past. Blow is irregular: blow - blew.

questions.after: the dark pipes and reached our tap.
questions.rule: Through shows movement inside something from one end to the other.
Command: Please + verb + object + adverb of manner.

questions.prompt: Make a simile about the pond.
questions.rule: A simile compares two things using like: shone like a mirror. Shone is the past of shine.

chat: What did you do on the rainy day?
options: I made paper boats and sailed them across the puddles.
I made paper boats and sail them across the puddles.
I maked paper boats and sailed them across the puddles.
questions.rule: Both verbs joined by and stay in the past: made (irregular) and sailed.

options: It rained heavily while I walking home.
It rained heavily while I was walking home.
It rained heavily while I were walking home.
questions.rule: The adverb heavily tells how it rained, and the past continuous needs was + -ing: I was walking.

options: As the drop rushed through the pipes, it hum softly like a song.
As the drop rushed through the pipes, it hummed softly like a song.
As the drop rushed through the pipes, it hummed softly as like a song.
questions.rule: Both actions are past (rushed, hummed). A simile uses like or as, never both.

options: The river flowed more faster than ever after the storm.
The river flowed faster than ever after the storm.
The river flowed fastly than ever after the storm.
questions.rule: Fast becomes faster; never add more to an -er word. Fastly is not a word.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Rushed how? Use the adverb rapidly.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Sink is irregular: sink - sank - sunk. Sinked is not a word.

questions.before: The drop rose into the sky, floated for days and finally
questions.rule: All the actions in the list are past (rose, floated), so the last one is past too: came.
Water is uncountable, so use as much ... as. As many is for countable nouns.
Time phrase + subject + verb + place: across Mumbai means all over the city.

questions.prompt: Make a simile about his voice.
questions.rule: A simile compares two different things with like: sweet like honey.

chat: How did the plants look after the rain?
questions.rule: After look meaning 'seem', use adjectives (fresh, bright), not adverbs.

options: Water dripped into it from the roof since all night.
Water drip into it from the roof all night.
Water dripped into it from the roof all night.
questions.rule: All night needs no since. Into shows the water going inside, and dripped is past.
